#30460. Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1533 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

It has been revealed that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Latest York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He mentioned he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

It has been revealed that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, stated music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

Industry observers note that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

According to recent reports, jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

According to recent reports, “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

It has been revealed that agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she remarked, but it highlighted cold.

Recent findings suggest that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova mentioned. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Recent findings suggest that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and upcoming construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova mentioned. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

According to recent reports, andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney mentioned.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Sources indicate that hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Industry observers note that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

Recent findings suggest that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

According to recent reports, his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

In a recent development, “Every week, I share newly introduced songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he stated. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

In a recent development, on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

According to recent reports, bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Recent findings suggest that kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

Industry observers note that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova mentioned she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

Sources indicate that so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova noted, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that on Nov.
  • As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He remarked that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

In a recent development, selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

For some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

It has been revealed that the latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Georgia-based homebuilder My Home Communities is expanding beyond its home state with new-home communities planned in South Carolina, Alabama and Northwest Florida, the manufacturer announced earlier this week.

The privately held builder, founded in 2018, will launch sales this month at Stonebrook in Gaffney, South Carolina, is planning an 89-homesite community in Summerdale, Alabama, and is preparing an initial presence along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton, Florida.

“Georgia has provided an incredible foundation for our company, and we’re excited to take what we’ve built here into upcoming markets,” stated Jacob Prather, president of My Home Communities. “Expanding into South Carolina, Alabama and Florida is about building relationships, creating new opportunities for homebuyers and establishing My Home Communities as a recognized homebuilding brand throughout the Southeast.”.

My Home Communities focused its first eight years on establishing a footprint across metro Atlanta and other Georgia markets, offering single-family homes and communities targeted to a wide range of buyers.

The company said continued investment in Georgia remains a core part of its strategy even as it exports its building processes and customer service model to other Southeast states.

The expansion is being supported by the Tamra Wade Team, backed by RE/MAX TRU, which is leading sales and marketing efforts for My Home Communities in the new markets. The team has worked with the builder for several years in Georgia, providing continuity as the tech giant introduces its brand to buyers outside the state.

In South Carolina, Stonebrook in Gaffney is preparing to launch sales in November 2026, with prices expected to start in the high $200,000s, according to the company. The community is My Home Communities’ first project in South Carolina.

In Alabama, The Retreat in Summerdale is planned as an 89-homesite community. Sales timing has not yet been announced. The organization mentioned the project will expand its reach into the Gulf Coast corridor, where fresh-home demand has been supported by employment growth and relative affordability compared to coastal metros.

In a recent development, in Northwest Florida, My Home Communities looks to start with two homesites along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton. Additional community details and sales timelines will be released later.

“Our growth is intentional, and we’re focused on finding the right opportunities in markets where we believe our homes and communities will resonate with buyers,” Prather mentioned. “With Stonebrook launching sales this month and additional communities planned in Alabama and Florida, we’re excited to introduce our brand to latest audiences.”.

The forum convened as outages across transportation, banking, telecommunications, and national security exposed vulnerabilities in the complex systems underpinning U.S. critical infrastructure. Because these systems are built, maintained, and operated by multiple stakeholders across domains, it is increasingly difficult to predict how they will behave when something goes wrong.

Anjana Rajan, CEO and Co-Founder of Atalanta, gave a presentation titled "Forward Deployed Formal Methods," which discussed Atalanta's learnings from the front lines on how to apply mathematical rigor to real world missions.

According to recent reports, "Over the last week, we have seen elected officials and leaders not know what caused these outages," mentioned Rajan. "There is a name for this phenomenon, and it's called the software understanding gap.".

It has been revealed that during her remarks, Rajan declared the launch of Ata, Atalanta's fresh formal verification language. Ata brings mathematical verification to the operators responsible for today's critical systems so they can verify how those systems will behave under normal, abnormal, or hostile conditions.

"How do I know my critical infrastructure will perform as intended, even when under attack?" Rajan remarked. "This is the fundamental challenge facing mission owners who need to know that the systems they depend on will work. Atalanta is already meeting this moment. ".

Recent findings suggest that atalanta is right now working across a range of critical infrastructure sectors, including defense, space, and energy. In August, Viasat revealed that it had used Atalanta's platform, Argo, to demonstrate improved resilience of satellite networks against modern warfare threats. Atalanta is also supporting the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission through its partnership with Idaho National Laboratory, bringing formal verification techniques to the development of autonomous nuclear reactors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pulley, a development technology company that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in latest funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company announced this week.

Recent findings suggest that the financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. Pulley said the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and newly introduced products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines.

Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.

Pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The company estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions.

Recent findings suggest that “The speed at which we build is one of the most key challenges facing America over the next decade,” mentioned Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”.

Pulley said it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The manufacturer reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time.

Recent findings suggest that pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction proposal reviews and coordination with local agencies. The firm also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building intends directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer said customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission.

In a recent development, with the new funding, Pulley looks to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs.

Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance issues earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during proposal check.

Lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing quickly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital aims and delay unit delivery into tight markets.

Tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and fresh capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private initiative review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing users multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Recent findings suggest that essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

According to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

If successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For owners: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

Industry observers note that “When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane said.

According to recent reports, delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the manufacturer’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.).

The way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

Sources indicate that “The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane said. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners rapidly.”.

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane stated.

According to recent reports, the performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

According to recent reports, DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this firm to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane said.

According to recent reports, house of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

This is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake mentioned.

According to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Industry observers note that ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

  • A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.
  • According to recent reports, in a complaint filed Nov.
  • WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.

According to recent reports, in a complaint filed Nov. 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.

WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.

In a recent development, according to the complaint, Heaps began working for WCL in November 2023 as a branch manager. In January 2024, he also took on internal technology responsibilities, including customer relationship management (CRM) administration, software development and systems integration. His employment ended in September 2025.

Heaps claims WCL classified him as a 1099 independent contractor while paying him a fixed recurring amount regardless of hours worked and still exercising control over his work. He alleges he reported to a manager, worked from an assigned office in Irvine, did not submit invoices, regularly worked more than 40 hours per week without overtime pay and did not receive his final paycheck after his employment ended.

Industry observers note that “This treatment was not merely occasional, but reflected Defendants’ pattern and practice of willfully misclassifying Defendants’ employees as independent contractors,” the lawsuit states.In a statement to HousingWire, Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Michael Sigall, who represent the plaintiff, noted they had filed “a class action lawsuit against West Capital Lending, Inc. alleging the company misclassified workers as independent contractors when they should have been treated as employees.”“As a result, workers were allegedly denied basic wage and hour protections California law guarantees. Hardworking people deserve to be paid every dollar they’ve earned, and we are committed to holding West Capital accountable,” they wrote.

WCL, which has about 1,900 sponsored LOs and originated about $10.8 billion year-to-date, has been the target of several lawsuits over its business and employment practices in recent years. Competitors, including loanDepot and Griffin Funding, along with former employees, have filed actions challenging the company’s model. WCL has denied wrongdoing in those cases.

Sources indicate that the 1099 independent contractor structure is also part of loanDepot’s ongoing lawsuit against WCL. In that case, loanDepot alleged that WCL misclassified about 600 loan officers as independent contractors, paying them on a 1099 basis and avoiding employment-related costs.

“loanDepot’s investigation has revealed that all of its former California loan originators poached by WCL who still hold California licenses to originate loans switched from operating under the standard MLO license issued by the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI), which requires mortgage loan originators to be employees of their sponsoring lender, to a ‘real estate salesperson with MLO endorsement’ license issued by the DRE [Department of Real Estate] after joining WCL,” the loanDepot complaint states.

The loanDepot complaint alleges that WCL’s California LOs perform exclusively mortgage loan origination duties, not real estate sales activities. WCL allegedly classifies its California originators as independent contractors while treating those in other states as employees. (WCL also sued loanDepot, alleging Truth in Lending Act violations).

California Labor Code Section 2775 codifies the so-called ABC test for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. However, Section 2778(c)(1) excludes qualifying real estate licensees from the ABC test and directs their classification to California Business and Professions Code Section 10032(b).

That provision allows real estate brokers and salespersons to establish their relationship as either employer-employee or independent contractor. For other purposes under the Labor Code, the Borello multifactor test, which is a more flexible, fact-specific analysis, generally applies.Under the ABC test, which applies to most workers, an individual is presumed to be an employee unless the hiring entity establishes all three conditions: The worker is free from the firm’s control and direction, both under the contract and in practice; performs work outside the usual course of the company’s business; and is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation or business of the same nature as the work performed.

In the Heaps case, the complaint asserts that WCL’s treatment of the plaintiff “cannot meet any part of the ABC Test and Defendants knew it.”.

Industry observers note that the DFPI referred questions about this licensing and employment model to the DRE, which did not respond to requests for comment. The Department of Industrial Relations, which enforces labor law, also did not respond to questions.

The use of 1099 models for loan originators and branch personnel has become a flashpoint in California, where some lenders argue that compliance-focused firms are at a competitive disadvantage.

Alan Pezeshkian, president of California-based House America Financial, stated he is not opposed to 1099 compensation structures in principle but is concerned about inconsistent application of labor and tax standards.

“When companies gain a competitive advantage by circumventing employment and tax laws, it creates an uneven playing field and penalizes those of us who make compliance a priority,” Pezeshkian mentioned. “Let’s call it what it is: when a company improperly classifies employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes and other employment obligations, that’s not innovation, that’s just gaming the system. And when that becomes a recruiting strategy, companies that follow the rules are effectively being punished for doing the right thing.”.

Troy Garris, co-managing partner at Garris Horn LLP, said the inquiry under many laws focuses on control versus independence.

“Under many laws, a worker is an employee if the business can dictate not just what is done, but how, when and where it is done, and by whom. Independent contractors, by contrast, run their own businesses: they set their own methods, use their own tools, take on the risk of profit or loss, and are free to work for other companies,” Garris mentioned. “Some laws make proving contractor status especially difficult, such as under California’s ABC test.”.

Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson, remarked hiring 1099 independent contractors, from a regulatory perspective, is a “dangerous game” because the definition of “employee” touches multiple regimes.

It has been revealed that “Regulation Z does not define employees,” Selden mentioned. “If a term is not defined within the regulation, you look to the contract and state law. So, then that’s gray.”Enhancement: This story has been updated to include a statement from the plaintiff’s attorneys.

  • Industry observers note that A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S.
  • Industry observers note that the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.

Industry observers note that A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

Industry observers note that the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

Sources indicate that “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, remarked in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In a recent development, in the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

It has been revealed that the study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

Industry observers note that all three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for upcoming clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

Industry observers note that at the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Ledger, a crypto wallet firm, noted it had experienced a security incident related to Optimizely, a third-party service used on its official website, but reassured its customers about the security of their devices and private keys.

In a post, Ledger remarked it was aware of a security incident impacting Optimizely, a third-party service provider used by many other sites as well.

Recent findings suggest that we are aware of a security incident affecting Optimizely, a third-party service used on https://t.co/d2pWxdG49X, alongside numerous other websites. Our team has remediated the issue, and the malicious code is no longer being served through our website. This incident does not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices. Your private keys remain protected by your Ledger device. For more information from Optimizely: https://t.co/CxzmBxYadb.

Website optimization platform Optimizely mentioned it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Optimizely stated that the vulnerable path has now been blocked, the injected code has been removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the concern and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring consumers that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

According to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

According to recent reports, the main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents mentioned.

According to recent reports, pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

In a recent development, pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly mentioned that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also noted the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Industry observers note that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” stated David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

Sources indicate that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.
  • In a recent development, the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.

In a recent development, the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation. It is likely one of the last bipartisan measures this Congress will vote on before the 120th Congress is sworn in shortly after the latest year.

Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.

BAAJA now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives, which is widely expected to vote on the measure before the new Congress is sworn in on January 3. However, the clock is ticking, as the House is already on Thanksgiving recess. That leaves about a month for the House to either pass the Senate’s version or reconcile any differences between the two chambers.

If the bill doesn’t reach President Trump’s desk by January 3, the process would have to start over with the new Congress, which would likely change some of its provisions.

Many affordable and multifamily projects that rely on federal funding or assistance face regulatory hurdles that most privately financed housing developments avoid.

These projects include those backed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Examples include housing built using public housing assistance, Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding, USDA housing loans, disaster relief funds and more.

Most notably, these federally backed housing projects must go through National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that don’t apply to most private- sector development projects.

According to recent reports, these reviews, critics argue, add an extra regulatory burden that can increase project timelines by a year or more. Critics further contend that NEPA and NHPA, while well-intentioned laws, are often used by NIMBY groups to delay or kill affordable housing development.

In response to these concerns, BAAJA would streamline NEPA reviews for housing development by:.

These changes would strengthen and expand provisions in the HOME Reform Act of 2025, a bill included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that exempted small federal housing projects of 15 units or less from NEPA review.

BAAJA would similarly streamline NHPA reviews and narrow which projects trigger a review, allowing redevelopment projects involving older buildings to move forward more promptly.

Additionally, the bill would streamline Clean Water Act reviews, in effect speeding up federal wetlands permitting by shortening review timelines and limiting certain EPA interventions and legal challenges. It would also shorten Endangered Species Act consultation timelines and give states a larger role in federal reviews to reduce permitting delays for residential developments on land with protected species or habitats.

Support for BAAJA spans much of the housing industry. Earlier this month, the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, Up for Growth Action and dozens of other housing organizations and homebuilder groups signed a letter urging the Senate to move the permitting reform package forward.

On Friday, National Association of REALTORS Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn noted in a statement she supports the legislation’s goal of streamlining “permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction and limit housing supply.”.

“These barriers affect everything from starter homes to multifamily rental housing, making it harder to meet the needs of buyers and renters alike,” McGahn stated.

Industry observers note that NAHB further argued that BAAJA would reduce land development costs and permitting delays, while also improving multifamily builders’ access to federal housing finance programs. In a statement following the Senate’s vote, NAHB Chairman Bill Owens said that the bill “will help builders deliver the affordable homes families need.”.

According to recent reports, “By cutting the regulatory costs and delays that drive up the price of construction, BAAJA will expand housing supply, lower costs for buyers and renters and increase access to affordable rental housing. With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay,” Owens said.

Housing is only a fraction of what BAAJA targets. It mainly aims to streamline the development of a wide range of federally backed projects, including:.

As it does for housing, BAAJA would scale back NEPA and other environmental reviews for these federal projects, while also including other measures to shorten permitting and approval timelines.

In the Senate, 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of the bill.

Senators Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were the only Republican Senators to vote against the legislation, largely because they feared it would undermine states’ rights.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, 31 Democrats voted against it. The legislation has drawn significant opposition from environmental groups concerned that its permitting changes could weaken environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel emissions.

Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, for example, argued that the bill “furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands and endangers wildlife.”.

Other critics of BAAJA worry that the bill’s permitting reforms could accelerate the development of more data centers, including on public lands.

Despite the ongoing opposition from environmental groups, BAAJA has bipartisan support in the House. For example, Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who backs the bill’s permitting provisions, countered these concerns by noting that it would also fast-track renewable energy development. He reiterated his support for the bill after it passed the Senate.

According to recent reports, “BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us,” Peters said in a statement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a manufacturer’s own work.

Sources indicate that menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Sources indicate that noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company mentioned.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company stated.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin remarked at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

It has been revealed that noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

According to recent reports, noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FRESH YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Payoneer, the global financial technology organization powering business growth across borders, today unveiled that it has received preliminary conditional approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to form PAYO Digital Bank, a national trust bank designed to support stablecoin functionality for global business. Today's approval creates a path for Payoneer to build a federally regulated foundation for the future of cross-border commerce, supporting the businesses as they adopt stablecoins and simplifying how they pay and get paid globally. PAYO Digital Bank is now able to operate in its organizational phase, while it seeks final approval to open for business.

It has been revealed that once PAYO Digital Bank receives final OCC approval to open and issue payment stablecoins, it looks to issue PAYO-USD, a fully reserved, GENIUS Act-compliant stablecoin. PAYO-USD, which will not be listed on exchanges, will serve as a balance within the Payoneer ecosystem that will drive interoperability between traditional and blockchain-based currencies. This delivers real-world utility, giving businesses access to safe stablecoin balances and allowing for frictionless movement into local currencies where they operate. This builds on Payoneer's existing network, delivering local currency payouts in 190+ markets.

"The promise of stablecoin is to simplify global commerce. That can only happen when stablecoin is useful in the markets where our customers operate," said Rob Morgan, CEO of PAYO Digital Bank. "Morer than one third of our customers already use stablecoin today. PAYO-USD is designed to improve the experience, making it seamless for businesses to convert their stablecoin balances into the local currencies needed to run their business, giving them more choice, faster movement of funds, and an easier way to transact globally.".

PAYO Digital Bank will offer a wide range of stablecoin services, allowing customers to hold stablecoin balances in bank-approved digital wallets, enable businesses to pay or be paid in a variety of third-party stablecoins, and convert their balances into fiat in the local markets where they operate. The bank will operate under direct federal oversight, enabling global businesses to adopt stablecoin payments from a safe and trusted partner.

In a recent development, payoneer is the financial platform for cross-border business and global payments. Payoneer empowers millions of businesses with the financial tools and services they need to grow and transact globally with confidence. Payoneer makes it easier for businesses, particularly in emerging markets, to connect to the global economy, pay and get paid across borders, manage their funds across multiple currencies, and grow their businesses.

For more information, visit https://www.payoneer.com/.

Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off.
  • Sources indicate that that shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation.
  • “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:09 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

Sources indicate that that shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

“As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari mentioned. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”.

Bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

Industry observers note that the first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to owners and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

“Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari remarked.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari mentioned.

In a recent development, the scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that “On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari stated. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”.

That thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari said.

Bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he stated: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly important as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”.

Industry News: Lock-in effect likely to keep HELOCs, second lien activity up through 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity.
  • According to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan.
  • According to recent reports, annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

According to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

According to recent reports, annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve Bank of Fresh York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

Sources indicate that as a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he stated.

Stratis noted the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

“Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis said. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

It has been revealed that matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

Sources indicate that “Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon noted. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a new roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

It has been revealed that tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his organization has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

Hutchens said borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

“Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, stated that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

“[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz said. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a fresh loan, he stated. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, said borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

Industry observers note that “The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen mentioned. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the new rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

Leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he remarked, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

For borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz remarked.

It has been revealed that adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, said home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a newly introduced mortgage.

Recent findings suggest that “A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson stated. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company revealed Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company remarked. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Sources indicate that owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company claims other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

It has been revealed that “At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The tech giant has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Sources indicate that fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the manufacturer in February.

On a recent podcast, Hoskinson stated, “Now I’m going from building Cardano to building on Cardano.”.
