‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.
  • Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.
  • The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that claims, “Do not search Amazon.”.

According to recent reports, the change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta released the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s newly introduced is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the tech giant had nothing to share.

Sources indicate that amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has stated Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

In a recent development, since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

Industry observers note that the business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Sources indicate that jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#30385. Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1193 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • It has been revealed that healthcare is the clearest example.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

It has been revealed that healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Sources indicate that venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an crucial regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

Recent findings suggest that as an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health looks and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

In a recent development, founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

According to recent reports, has the founder or manufacturer addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

In a recent development, these challenges make the earliest stages of tech giant formation particularly key. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

Sources indicate that at Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

In a recent development, that means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

AI and newly introduced distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

In a recent development, the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Sources indicate that moving swiftly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

In a recent development, for investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a firm needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

It has been revealed that the most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

Industry observers note that for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare is the clearest example. A manufacturer can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

  • In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

Industry observers note that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

Sources indicate that I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

In a recent development, I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying upcoming things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

In a recent development, every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a major deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Recent findings suggest that look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a massive believer in having a vision and building a proposal to get there. I’ve also learned that a fresh calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

Recent findings suggest that for the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to overhaul the whole organization all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

According to recent reports, jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he stated, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Sources indicate that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

Sources indicate that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

In a recent development, hyperliquid Anthropic trading market has surged to $1.7 billion in daily volume, pushing the contract ahead of Ethereum on the platform. The surge comes just as Hong Kong’s financial regulator adds Hyperliquid to its suspicious virtual asset trading platform list.

Industry observers note that the ANT perpetual contract recorded $1.727 billion in trading volume over 24 hours on November 20. This has placed it second among Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets, behind Bitcoin but ahead of Ethereum.

Open interest also climbed to $259 million as traders built substantial positions rather than simply passing through short-term trades. The figures put Anthropic market in Hyperliquid among the exchange’s most active markets, despite tracking a tech giant outside the traditional crypto sector.

Sources indicate that just a day earlier, Anthropic ranked 17th among Hyperliquid perpetual contracts by trading volume. It then climbed to second place as activity accelerated around Anthropic’s public market debut. Its $1.727 billion turnover was 1.88 times Ethereum’s trading volume during the same period. Only Bitcoin attracted more activity, recording $5.139 billion.

According to recent reports, the shift also displays how much Hyperliquid’s trading activity now extends beyond crypto-native assets. Six of the exchange’s top ten perpetual markets by volume were linked to traditional financial assets.

These included Anthropic, the XYZ100 technology index, the S&P 500, Nvidia, a leveraged semiconductor ETF, and South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix. Together, those six contracts generated $4.269 billion in volume, accounting for 38.1% of the top ten’s combined turnover.

Sources indicate that ANT’s market has also attracted significant leverage. The contract allows traders to speculate on Anthropic’s share price using crypto collateral, without purchasing or owning the underlying shares.

Unlike conventional stock markets, the perpetual contract continues trading around the clock. This gives traders a venue to react to developments outside Nasdaq’s regular trading hours. This flexibility has helped attract activity as traders position themselves around major developments affecting the artificial intelligence sector.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

In a recent development, hyperliquid has demonstrated how much demand exists for trading assets beyond traditional crypto. Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a different opportunity: bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a much larger decentralized finance ecosystem.

Industry observers note that the project is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. Its goal is to let BTC holders move beyond simply holding their coins, opening access to faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications.

Recent findings suggest that that ambition is attracting considerable presale interest. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.29 million, with its token right now priced at just $0.01368760. More than 114,000 participants have joined the presale, giving the project considerable early fundraising momentum.

Staking is another major attraction, with the project offering rewards of up to 35% APY. That gives early participants an additional incentive to accumulate HYPER before its exchange debut, although actual rewards depend on the staking terms and participation.

Time is also becoming a factor. Bitcoin Hyper has scheduled its presale conclusion for November 26, putting its anticipated launch just days away. With the token still available below two cents, the approaching deadline could intensify demand among investors looking to secure an early position.

It has been revealed that the trading surge comes against a growing regulatory problem for Hyperliquid. Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission added Hyperliquid and Hyperliquid Hong Kong to its suspicious virtual asset trading platforms list. The regulator specifically identified the platform’s trading interface at app.hyperliquid.xyz, stating that the entity was not licensed by the SFC.

🚨 Hong Kong’s SFC has added Hyperliquid to its Alert List of unlicensed, "suspicious" crypto platforms.First Singapore's MAS in June, now Hong Kong. Asian regulators are turning up the heat on decentralized perp DEXs.

The watchdog suspects the platform of operating, holding itself out as operating, or actively marketing an unlicensed virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public.

The warning puts Hyperliquid under scrutiny in one of Asia’s most important financial centers. Hong Kong has spent recent years developing a licensing framework for crypto exchanges, requiring platforms serving local investors to obtain regulatory authorization.

The SFC also warned that investors using unlicensed platforms could lose their entire investment if an operator collapses, suffers a hack, or misappropriates customer assets.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

Recent findings suggest that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

It has been revealed that proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration strategy and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

Industry observers note that the technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It highlights how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:.

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

According to recent reports, A no vote would stop the whole strategy. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 revealed an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Recent findings suggest that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

In a recent development, mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

In a recent development, the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC demonstrated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

It has been revealed that the spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

It has been revealed that at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

It has been revealed that so Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

Industry observers note that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the strategy goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

  • Sources indicate that jeff Bezos states Nvidia should look inside the tech giant for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success.
  • In a recent development, “If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 5:07 pm.

Sources indicate that jeff Bezos states Nvidia should look inside the tech giant for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

In a recent development, “If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos remarked. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”.

According to recent reports, nvidia’s board notes it has no looks to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place promptly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He noted he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, nvidia revealed Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the Fresh York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is serving as interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”.

Industry observers note that the Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He mentioned he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”.

According to recent reports, huang himself stated in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the organization.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”.

Recent findings suggest that in case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”.

#30379. Bitwise CEO Urges Americans to Hold Crypto as Banking Giants Go Down

Bitwise CEO Urges Americans to Hold Crypto as Banking Giants Go Down

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (325 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following multiple technical outages at major U.S.
  • In a recent X post, Horsley pointed to the weaknesses of traditional financial systems, especially in the context of the world's growing reliance on technology.
  • "Consider having some stablecoins or crypto just in case.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following multiple technical outages at major U.S. banks that left thousands of people unable to access banking services or make transactions, Bitwise CEO Hunter Horsley has urged Americans to keep some of their funds in crypto or stablecoins as a backup proposal.

In a recent X post, Horsley pointed to the weaknesses of traditional financial systems, especially in the context of the world's growing reliance on technology.

"Rolling bank outages in the AI era," he remarked.

"Consider having some stablecoins or crypto just in case.".

Large U.S. financial institutions such as JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo experienced widespread complaints about technical outages on Nov. 16.

Customers said they were having trouble logging into their online accounts, viewing their balances and conducting transactions.

According to Fox News, the incident affected some of the biggest banking names in the U.S. Thousands of people reported the glitch via the outage-tracking platform Downdetector.

Zelle, a popular payment service that people use in the U.S. to transfer funds between bank accounts, was also reportedly affected.

Sources indicate that as of the evening of Nov. 16, Chase had fixed the technical glitch, according to the bank. It remarked transactions were back to normal.

Sources indicate that the outage reports initially pointed to multiple banking systems going down at the same time. But further investigation revealed that problems at Chase spilled over into transactions with other banks. However, the Zelle app itself continued to work.

It has been revealed that stablecoins such as USDT and USDC aim to track the value of the U.S. dollar as closely as possible. They can be an option for those looking to hold digital funds without the extreme price fluctuations of crypto assets like Bitcoin.

For instance, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, participants in blockchain networks can transfer dollar-based stablecoins 24/7. However, cashing them out into traditional money may still require access to traditional financial institutions.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

Sources indicate that “The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

According to recent reports, “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom remarked, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We indicated up and mentioned, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

Industry observers note that “We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

According to recent reports, the region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

Recent findings suggest that “And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.

Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI tech giant’s blockbuster Wall Street debut.

Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded.At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the organization’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock swiftly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

In a recent development, anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks.

Jeff Bezos has a space tech giant, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

In a recent development, amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos noted a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos noted the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

It has been revealed that “We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the company's selling spree highlights no signs of slowing down.

According to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov. 18.

The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining company throughout 2026.

Lookonchain estimates that MARA has already sold a staggering 40,581 BTC this year, generating approximately $3.03 billion at an average selling price of $74,446 per coin.

However, it remains unclear whether the latest 366 BTC transfer represents another completed sale or an internal movement of funds.

MARA's aggressive selling strategy is confirmed by its latest quarterly financial disclosures.

Sources indicate that according to its Nov. 9 SEC filing, the company sold approximately 26,984 BTC for $1.9 billion during the first nine months of 2026.

Following the end of September, MARA liquidated another 13,597 BTC at an average price of approximately $81,039, raising an additional $1.1 billion.

These transactions bring its total disclosed Bitcoin sales to 40,581 BTC.

Notably, the company used $750 million from its latest sales to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.

Interestingly, MARA has explicitly signaled that it intends to continue selling Bitcoin as part of a broader shift in its corporate strategy.

However, it began allowing sales of newly mined Bitcoin in 2025 before expanding the policy in 2026 to include coins already held on its balance sheet.

In its latest shareholder letter, MARA remarked it plans to continue monetizing Bitcoin to strengthen its financial flexibility.

The company specifically identified artificial intelligence infrastructure, upcoming convertible debt obligations and potential share repurchases as reasons for building up cash reserves.

The selling comes as MARA faces considerable pressure on its core mining business.

Third-quarter revenue declined 35% year over year to $164.2 million, compared to $252.4 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data demonstrates the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

Sources indicate that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot highlights its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham claims those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

Industry observers note that the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It highlights how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

It has been revealed that binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now reveals:.

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what owners hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

Recent findings suggest that the striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Recent findings suggest that compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, revealed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

It has been revealed that not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance indicates it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

According to recent reports, what the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

In a recent development, binance notes the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

According to recent reports, what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

It has been revealed that binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia, and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week, and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday.

Even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same, and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

The nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report remarked. After all, the war is ongoing, and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island.

According to recent reports, “Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency or a lack of anxiety, but [the war] is still a pretty major deal,” mentioned oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm.

Recent findings suggest that “What I worry is if the Iranians feel they have to make people anxious again. Do they view it in their strategic interest to create more anxiety?” Pickering noted to Fortune. “I think we’ll have this uneasy conflict going on with Iran for a bunch of 2027.”.

Sources indicate that between alternative pipelines and routes, and U.S. escorts through Hormuz, Middle Eastern oil exports are approaching 90% of their prewar levels despite the ongoing military strikes, mentioned Pavel Molchanov, Raymond James energy analyst. “This indicates that the oil market has become acclimated to periodic flare-ups, just as long as there is no return to all-out war,” he added. “That said, the lack of a U.S.-Iran deal still translates into a hefty risk premium.”.

Recent findings suggest that because of seasonal demand dips, rising Middle Eastern exports, and President Donald Trump’s emphasis on de-escalating the war since the midterm congressional elections, global oil prices have fallen below the $100 per barrel threshold, even though the global benchmark remains high at more than $90. After all, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is dangerously depleted at a 44-year low, and the world has cumulatively lost 2.8 billion barrels of oil over nearly nine months, the IEA report stated.

The Iran war has triggered record-high fuel spikes in the U.S. But keep in mind that the U.S. leads the world in oil output, presently producing an all-time high of more than 14 million barrels daily. The rest of the world is left even more at the mercy of the war, and the price spikes and physical shortages are amplified, especially in Asia and Africa.

More than 4 billion people—roughly half the global population—depended on the Middle East for over 30% of its oil supplies. And about 80% of Middle Eastern oil exports were destined for Asia before the war.

Even as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Iraq move to build pipelines to divert oil supplies through alternate routes, those projects will take years, and long-term Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would maintain uncertainty going forward.

In a recent development, “That’s not a particularly comforting outlook to the consumers of Middle East crude,” Pickering noted. “The finish matters, and I don’t think we have visibility on what the finish looks like.”.

According to recent reports, the Americas are leading the increase in oil production—the U.S., Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Guyana, and now Venezuela—as well as a slate of African nations. And more countries are investing in renewable energy and electrification for electric vehicles.

Recent findings suggest that birol and the IEA forecast that renewables—solar, wind, and batteries—are picking up momentum throughout the world even as the globe falls short of its climate change goals. Nuclear power also is gaining steam. EV sales are projected to rise in most of the world next year—less so in the U.S.—in part because of cheaper, subsidized Chinese EVs being exported worldwide.

Global oil demand is now expected to peak by 2030 and slowly decline from there, the IEA remarked. Natural gas demand will grow through the mid-2030s and plateau.

According to recent reports, the IEA outlook noted that August was the hottest month ever on record worldwide and a strong El Niño could add to weather-related strains heading into 2027. “High energy prices and shortfalls in fertilizer supply are creating hazards for food security,” the report stated. “Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and air pollutants from fuel combustion remain dangerously high. Energy geopolitics are fracturing, and trade restrictions are on the rise. Trust is in short supply. Each vulnerability deepens the others.”.

That is why—more than ever—the world requires “credible road maps to phase out fossil fuels, backed by the public finance needed to ensure a fast and fair transition,” stated David Tong, global industry lead at Oil Change International.

Sources indicate that “Fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures,” Tong added. “After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the firm prepares to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Industry observers note that panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, mentioned Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he mentioned. “We have to take upcoming technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

According to recent reports, while the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky remarked. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Industry observers note that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky remarked Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The manufacturer must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that the organization has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round confirmed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Industry observers note that seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently declared looks for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky noted.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that the first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, remarked while speaking with Fortune‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.
  • Ioffe’s organization uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, remarked while speaking with Fortune‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Ioffe’s organization uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely.

“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe mentioned.

That prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too promptly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported, HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear strategy for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with consultants to understand why. He believes AI can help executives get answers in days rather than months.

In a recent development, ioffe didn’t set out to compete with consulting firms. At 19, he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform, then shifted Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies, becoming one of OpenAI’s early partners along the way.

He started to notice a pattern: companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem, then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it. In his experience, the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time.

Recent findings suggest that that prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing the problems companies were trying to solve. Ioffe pointed to a major software tech giant whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why.

According to recent reports, before AI can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it first needs to understand what’s happening inside a company. Arist’s agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions, and weigh responses against information such as an employee’s tenure, performance, and past engagement scores. Ioffe said that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization. The agents will also push back, he said, if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want.

But gathering that information could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an AI agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.

Ioffe argued that employees may actually be more candid with AI agents than with another person, making it easier for companies to uncover problems that might otherwise go unreported.

“Turns out that humans are not that good at listening,” he quipped.

Rather than replacing executives or consultants, Ioffe sees AI’s biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster.

“If you can get to the truth much faster, then a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup,” Ioffe stated.

"Modern platforms encourage the opposite of this, leading to more irresponsible behavior," Buterin added.

Ether was trading at $1,808 on Wednesday.

Buterin has written about housing and urban planning before. He has supported the YIMBY movement for denser development in cities for several years.

Industry observers note that in 2022, Buterin argued for a land value tax. According to him, such a tax would lower the upfront cost of buying a home and discourage speculation on vacant lots.

In 2025, the Ethereum co-founder called the housing market a "confusing market of peculiar NFTs." According to Buterin, what is really being sold under the label of square footage is the right to live in a particular city. At the time, he also stated that legalizing dense development speeds up the economy and benefits even people who prefer single-family homes.

The development points out that Russia has taken decisive action to deepen the integration of the crypto market with traditional finance. The debut indicates surging retail interest in cryptocurrency amid regulatory evolution.

In a recent development, it signals a strategic shift in how traditional exchanges handle digital assets. Accommodating retail clients signals growing confidence in the crypto market’s maturity. This highlights rising demand for coordinated exposure to crypto assets within Russia’s capital markets.

The announcement introduces new entry gateways that give retail investors organized access to the crypto market, redefining how these assets are traded locally and internationally.

Recent findings suggest that in the past, crypto in Russia operated in a highly restrictive, complex regulatory environment. Now, the regulator is moving toward a balance between investor freedom and financial stability. In July, the central bank opened the door to crypto for companies to facilitate global trade. Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first-100-days agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while it’s the responsibility of the U.S.
  • The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power.
  • Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while it’s the responsibility of the U.S. Department of the Treasury to finance the interest on the $40 trillion national debt, it is members of both parties in Congress who have added to Uncle Sam’s borrowing.With the Democrats winning a wave of seats in the midterm elections, everyone from Wall Street analysts to CEOs of America’s largest companies are wondering what a more divided government will mean.Budget watchdogs are doing the same, and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) has put a number on how much the Democrats’ strategy for their first 100 days will cost.

The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power. Hakeem Jeffries, nominated by Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House, wrote in November that they aim to “reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs, and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran.”.

Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year.

The CRFB estimates that, in total, the “first 100 days” policies would cost $4.1 trillion through 2037. Without offsets (spending cuts or revenue increases used to balance latest policies), $4.9 trillion would be added to the debt burden over the next decade, including interest costs.

Recent findings suggest that but the factor analysts—and budget hawks—really care about is the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio. This describes the level of borrowing a nation has relative to its economic growth, and therefore its ability to service that borrowing. At the moment, it stands at around 121%, per the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

In a recent development, economists suggest that if this balance were to tip further, then U.S. lenders may begin demanding higher premiums to offset the risk associated with the borrowing—sparking a bond crisis.

The House Democrats’ policies would increase the debt-to-GDP ratio to 135% by 2037 without offsets, versus 125% of GDP under an adjusted Congressional Budget Office baseline, the CRFB added.

The budget watchdog does offer some alternatives for how revenue to offset these proposals could be generated, though the reforms are unlikely to be popular with voters.

“Repealing the One Massive Beautiful Bill Act’s (OBBBA) tax cuts for high earners would generate about $2 trillion of savings—enough to offset an agenda scaled back by half,” the budget watchdog wrote.

“Repealing all of the tax cuts and spending increases in OBBBA—including its low-income and middle-class tax cuts—would generate about $7 trillion. That would be enough to pay for the First 100 Days agenda 1.7 times over.”.

The CRFB broke down each aspect of the proposals.

Starting first with the policies that could save money, the CRFB pointed to Iran. It noted that while ending the conflict would not immediately reduce deficits, it would likely avoid increases in military and defense spending. Continuing the war in Iran, the committee writes, costs approximately $30 billion a year and could be avoided.

It has been revealed that regarding policy costs for 2027–37, removing Trump’s tariffs leaves the largest budget hole. This represents $1.8 trillion in total, from repealing Section 301 tariffs (costing $955 billion alone) and Section 232 tariffs ($780 billion) to undoing Section 338 tariffs on certain Canadian goods ($35 billion).

Reversing the OBBBA health provisions would cost $1.6 trillion by 2037, the committee adds, including $600 billion to cancel provider tax and state-directed payment limits, as well as $485 billion to remove Medicaid work requirements. Reversing SNAP provisions would cost $250 billion over the next 10 years.

Increasing the deficit would also mean larger interest payments on the debt, the CRFB added—some $840 billion over the next 10 years.

‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code
